Cellars
sĕl´ẽrz
n. pl. (storehouses for wine and oil under royal charge — Hebrew otsar, a treasury)
Latin cellarium, a storeroom, from cella, a small chamber. The Hebrew word rendered cellars is the ordinary word for treasury or store.

Biblical Definition

Cellars occur in the Authorized Version in one passage: the roll of David's stewards at the end of Chronicles' account of his reign. “And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite” (1Ch 27:27), and “over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baalhanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash” (1Ch 27:28). The list is long and unglamorous — men set over herds, camels, asses, flocks, fields, vineyards, olives, wine and oil, each named with his town. Scripture bothers to record it, and the fact is instructive. A kingdom is administered, and God permits the register of its storerooms into holy writ alongside the psalms of its king. Two chapters later David gathers the whole and gives it away for the house of God, praying, “who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1Ch 29:14). That is the theology of the cellars. The store existed, it was carefully kept by named men, and the king who owned it confessed it was never his. The ordinary rule for every believer follows the same shape: “Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase” (Pro 3:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a cellar as a room under a building, used as a repository of liquors, provisions and other stores for a family.

expand to see more

CEL'LAR, n. A room under a building, and usually under ground, used as a repository of liquors, provisions and other stores for a family.

CEL'LARAGE, n. The room or space for cellars; cellars in general.

STORE, n. A large number or quantity; a stock provided; provisions accumulated.

STEW'ARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns and superintend the other servants.

Modern Corruption

Administration and ownership are confused, so that the man who keeps the store forgets he is a steward, and the man who dislikes stores despises the keeping of them.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is stewardship as an actual occupation. Scripture names the men who kept David's wine and oil, town by town, and preserves their names next to the psalms. Ordinary competent administration — counting, storing, keeping, handing on — is a service God notices and records, and a church that honours only the visible ministries has lost something the Chronicler thought worth writing down.

The temptation of the storehouse is named elsewhere in Scripture and is worth setting beside this list. The rich fool pulled down his barns to build greater and said to his soul, take thine ease; God called him a fool that night. The difference between his barns and David's cellars is not the size of the store but the sentence spoken over it. David's was, of thine own have we given thee. Where that sentence is not said, a full cellar becomes the ground of a false security, and the fuller it is the deeper the lie.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew otsar (H214), a treasury, storehouse — 1 Chronicles 27:27-28, and often of the treasuries of the house of the LORD.

expand to see more

Hebrew otsar (H214) — a treasury or store; 1 Chronicles 27:27-28, Malachi 3:10 of the storehouse for the tithe.

Hebrew yayin (H3196) and shemen (H8081) — wine and oil, the two great stores of an agricultural kingdom.

Hebrew shiqmah (H8256) — sycomore; the tree of the low plains, kept by Baalhanan the Gederite.

The passage is a register of stewards, each named with his town — ordinary administration recorded in Scripture.

1 Chronicles 29:14 supplies the theology of every storehouse: of thine own have we given thee.

Usage

"“Over the cellars of oil was Joash” — a steward named in holy writ."

"“Of thine own have we given thee” — the sentence that must be said over a full store."

"“Honour the LORD… with the firstfruits of all thine increase”."
